meta.name: Thanksgiving Dog Safety: What Dogs Can Eat, What's Dangerous and What to Do
meta.title_tag: Thanksgiving Dog Safety: What Dogs Can Eat & What to Do
meta.excerpt: Plain, boneless, skinless turkey and plain vegetables are fine for most dogs in small portions. Cooked bones, fatty skin and gravy, onion and garlic in stuffing, raisins, rising bread dough and sugar-free desserts are not. Here's a dish-by-dish guide and what to do if your dog gets into dinner.
meta.meta_description: Which Thanksgiving foods dogs can eat, why stuffing, gravy and cooked turkey bones are risky, and what to do if your dog raids the table or the trash.
meta.author: Kailun Zhang

hero.alt: Thanksgiving table with roast turkey, bones, stuffing with onions, gravy, raisins and pie — the holiday foods that put dogs at risk

body_html:
Quick Answer: Plain, boneless, skinless turkey and plain vegetables are fine for most dogs in small portions. The bigger risks are cooked bones and the carcass in the trash, fatty skin and gravy, onion and garlic in stuffing, raisins, rising bread dough and sugar-free desserts. If your dog already ate something risky, don't wait for symptoms: contact your veterinarian, or your nearest emergency vet or an animal poison control center right away. What to do now ↓

Dog Got Into Thanksgiving Dinner? Start Here

Many Thanksgiving problems show up late: bones can cause trouble hours to days later (FDA), pancreatitis up to 4 days later (Pet Poison Helpline) and onion or garlic anemia 3–5 days later (Merck Veterinary Manual). A dog that seems fine tonight may not be.

  1. Secure the rest. Move the carcass, plates and trash out of reach.
  2. Call now. Don't wait for symptoms: contact your veterinarian, or your nearest emergency vet or an animal poison control center right away.
  3. Have the recipe or box handy, but don't let this delay the call. Note the time and your dog's weight. You'll be asked whether the dish had onion, garlic, raisins, xylitol, chocolate or alcohol, and roughly how much is gone.
  4. Skip home remedies unless the vet or poison control team says otherwise: don't make your dog vomit, and don't feed bread "to cushion" a bone. Pet Poison Helpline warns that hydrogen peroxide can injure the gut.

Go straight to an emergency clinic for choking (gagging, drooling, pawing at the mouth), retching without bringing anything up, a swollen belly, sudden weakness or wobbliness, tremors or a seizure, collapse, unconsciousness or trouble breathing (Merck, Cornell, FDA). Calling ahead lets the clinic prepare (Merck).

Timing varies by source and by dog. For anything marked "call now," don't wait for signs: contact your veterinarian, or your nearest emergency vet or an animal poison control center right away.

Can Dogs Eat Turkey? The Parts That Are Fine and the Parts That Aren't

Plain, boneless, skinless turkey is generally safe for dogs in small portions (AVMA), but the holiday roast is rarely plain: it's rubbed with butter or oil and often cooked with onions and garlic inside (AKC). Carve your dog's share from the breast, since VCA lists dark turkey meat with the fatty foods that can cause pancreatitis; pick out bone slivers and skip the fatty skin (AKC, FDA). Keep extras within 10% of your dog's daily calories (VCA, AKC).

Turkey Bones, the Carcass and the Trash Can

Cooked poultry bones are brittle (AKC), and the FDA warns that bones from a raided carcass can lodge in a dog's esophagus, stomach or windpipe or cause severe internal injuries. The trash adds more: trussing string can cut holes in the intestine (Cornell), corn cobs top the list of objects dogs swallow (ASPCA), and mylar snack bags can suffocate a curious dog (FDA).

Bag the carcass, bones, string and packaging, and put them in a closed bin outdoors or behind a closed door (AVMA). If your dog swallowed any of it, call your vet now, before vomiting starts: gut tissue cut off from its blood supply for more than a few hours can die (VCA). Corn kernels off the cob are fine (AKC; see our corn guide).

Stuffing, Gravy and Casseroles: Where Onion and Garlic Hide

Pet Poison Helpline's Dr. Renee Schmid calls stuffing "a potential trifecta of dangers": onions, garlic and sometimes raisins. Onion and garlic also hide in casseroles (including green bean casserole's fried-onion topping), mashed potatoes and meat seasonings (Pet Poison Helpline, AKC), so check labels on gravy mixes, boxed stuffing and seasoning packets.

Every form counts: raw, cooked or powdered (VCA). Garlic is 3–5 times more toxic than onion, and concentrated forms such as powder and dry onion soup mix are most often linked to poisoning in dogs (Merck); one teaspoon of garlic powder equals about eight fresh cloves (VCA). Japanese breeds such as Akitas and Shiba Inus are more sensitive (Pet Poison Helpline). Stomach upset is common (VCA), but the serious damage is to red blood cells, and signs such as weakness, fast breathing and red or brown urine usually appear a few days later (Merck). If your dog ate a dish made with onion or garlic, call your vet or an emergency vet right away. See our onion and garlic guides.

Raisins and currants turn up in stuffing (Pet Poison Helpline), baked goods and trail mix (VCA) and some cranberry sauces (AKC). There's no well-established toxic dose, and some dogs are poisoned by small amounts (VCA). See our grapes and raisins and cranberry guides.

Turkey Skin, Gravy and Ham: Fat and Pancreatitis

Butter, bacon, drippings, gravy and meat scraps can trigger pancreatitis (Pet Poison Helpline), which the FDA calls potentially life-threatening, and AVMA warns that sometimes even a small amount can cause it. AKC lists ham among Thanksgiving foods to avoid, and Merck lists trash raids as a common risk factor. Signs include vomiting, belly pain, diarrhea, fever, shaking and weakness (FDA), sometimes with a "praying position," rear end up (VCA).

Merck reports higher rates in Miniature Schnauzers, Yorkshire Terriers, Cocker Spaniels, Dachshunds and Poodles, though VCA says there's no breed predisposition. If your dog raided the drippings, call your vet for advice, and go in if vomiting or belly pain starts.

Rising Dough, Pumpkin Pie, Chocolate and Drinks

Raw yeast dough is an emergency: it keeps rising in the stomach while the yeast makes alcohol (Merck); early signs are unproductive retching and a swollen belly, then wobbliness. Sourdough starter and frozen dough that rises before baking count too (Pet Poison Helpline). If the package lists yeast, or you're not sure, treat it as rising dough and call your vet right away. Baked bread is different (see our bread guide).

Pie: nutmeg can upset the stomach and is mainly a concern in large amounts (Pet Poison Helpline, ASPCA), so if your dog got into the spice jar, call your vet right away. The bigger pie risks are fat, sugar and xylitol, also labeled birch sugar or wood sugar (FDA; more in our Halloween guide).

Chocolate strength varies: by Merck's figures, cocoa powder and baking chocolate carry roughly 7 to 13 times the theobromine and caffeine of milk chocolate, and semisweet and dark chocolate about 2.5 times. Don't try to work out whether your dog ate "enough." With the recipe in hand, call your vet or an emergency vet right away. See our chocolate guide.

Drinks, brine and nuts. Alcohol, including boozy desserts, acts fast (Merck); Schmid told AAHA that alcohol poisoning can follow "just a few laps." Dogs also readily lap up turkey brine, which can cause salt poisoning (Pet Poison Helpline). Macadamias and moldy leftovers can cause tremors (Merck). For any of these, call your vet or an emergency vet right away.

Build a Dog-Safe Thanksgiving Plate

Set your dog's share aside before anything gets butter, salt, gravy or seasoning (ASPCA). Plain options (AKC unless noted):

  • Boneless, skinless turkey breast (AVMA)
  • Green beans and peas, not creamed
  • Sweet potato or boiled or baked potato, with no butter or marshmallows
  • Pure pumpkin purée, not pie filling
  • Apple slices without the core (AKC, Tufts), or carrots (Tufts)

Dogs that have had pancreatitis should get their vet's okay first.

Guests, Doors and Decorations

  • Brief guests, especially kids: no feeding the dog (VCA, AKC).
  • Keep bags and coats up high. They can hold medications, among the most common poisoning calls (ASPCA, Pet Poison Helpline), and cannabis edibles (Pet Poison Helpline).
  • Block off the kitchen when no one's watching (VCA), and give nervous dogs a quiet room or crate (AVMA).
  • Watch the door while collecting coats, and keep microchip registration current (AVMA).
  • Decorations: corn cobs, pine cones and gourds can cause choking or blockage (AVMA). Bittersweet can upset the stomach, candles can burn, and flameless-candle batteries can cause corrosive injury if swallowed (Pet Poison Helpline).

Thanksgiving Week Checklist

  • Monday–Tuesday, November 23–24: Check your vet's holiday hours and find the nearest 24-hour emergency clinic.
  • Wednesday, November 25: Keep brine, rising dough and cooling pies behind a closed door.
  • Thursday, November 26: Set aside your dog's plain portion, brief guests, keep bags up and empty the trash during the day (ASPCA).
  • Friday, November 27: Bag and remove the carcass, bones and string; toss moldy leftovers out of reach.

Written by Kailun Zhang, who is not a veterinarian. This guide summarizes the veterinary and poison-control sources listed below and isn't a substitute for advice from your vet.

Frequently Asked Questions

What Thanksgiving foods can dogs safely eat?

Small portions of plain, boneless, skinless turkey breast and plain vegetables such as green beans, sweet potato and pumpkin purée (AVMA, AKC), set aside before any butter, gravy, onion or garlic goes on.

My dog ate a cooked turkey bone. What should I do?

Don't wait for symptoms: contact your veterinarian, or your nearest emergency vet or an animal poison control center right away. Cooked bones can splinter, lodge in the gut or cause internal injuries, sometimes hours to days later (AKC, FDA). Don't give bread or other home remedies, or try to make your dog vomit, unless your vet tells you to.

How long after eating Thanksgiving food will a dog get sick?

It depends on the food, so call before signs appear. Xylitol can drop blood sugar within 30 minutes and alcohol act within 30–60 minutes (Merck); raw dough usually acts within an hour but can take several hours (Pet Poison Helpline). Chocolate usually takes 6–12 hours, raisin-related kidney failure 24–72 hours and onion or garlic anemia a few days (Merck). Bones can cause trouble hours to days later (FDA), and pancreatitis up to 4 days (Pet Poison Helpline).

Can dogs eat stuffing or dressing, even boxed stuffing mix?

No. Most stuffing contains onion and garlic, and some recipes add raisins (Pet Poison Helpline). Boxed mixes and seasoning packets can contain onion or garlic powder, the concentrated forms Merck links most often to poisoning. If your dog ate some, call your vet or an emergency vet right away.

Can dogs eat cranberry sauce?

Not the holiday kind. Cranberry sauce is high in sugar, and some recipes add grapes, raisins, currants or alcohol (AKC). Plain cranberries are the better way to share. If the sauce had raisins or alcohol, call your vet or an emergency vet right away.

Can dogs eat pumpkin pie?

Skip it. Pie is fatty and sugary, sugar-free versions may contain xylitol, and nutmeg is a concern in large amounts (Pet Poison Helpline). Plain pumpkin purée is the dog-friendly version (AKC). If your dog ate sugar-free pie or a lot of any pie, call your vet or an emergency vet right away.
